title: Why the Holidays are Gaming's Biggest Season and Its Riskiest
summary: Holiday traffic surges in gaming hide the attacks riding along with them. Learn how to protect capacity and catch credential stuffing without slowing down players.
body_markdown:
Every gaming company circles the same week on the calendar. New consoles get unwrapped. Lapsed players wander back from winter break. Battle passes and limited skins, released right when holiday gift cards hit wallets, drive some of the biggest sales spikes of the year.


Your infrastructure team circles the same week too, mostly because somebody always ends up writing the patch note that says “fixed: an entire studio’s worth of accounts got hijacked.”


The traffic that makes December your best month is nearly indistinguishable from the traffic trying to rob you blind. A login surge on December 26th could be a few million people opening presents, or it could be a credential stuffing attack that picks the one day your dashboards are too busy to notice. Gift card redemptions spike right alongside gift card fraud. A server buckling under real demand looks exactly like one going down to a DDoS attack, at least until someone’s pinged at 3am to figure out which.


Most studios still run this as two separate fire drills: Ops watching capacity and security watching for threats. A surge gives an attacker the one thing they need most: cover. Nobody launches an attack on a quiet Tuesday in March when every anomaly stands out. They wait for the week when “a lot of traffic” and “an attack” look like the same line on the same graph.


## What Peak Season Actually Looks like Inside a Gaming Company


The account surge cuts both ways: new signups on one side and dormant accounts “waking up” on the other. Players who haven’t touched the game since last summer hit the “forgot password” button in volumes that make your authentication teams wince.


Commerce compounds it. Checkout queues, entitlement checks, and inventory databases take on write volumes they won’t see again for another year, right as the gift card balances are burning a hole in every wallet.


And underneath it all, most studios have quietly frozen their deployment pipeline. Code freezes make sense. Nobody wants to ship a bug the one week revenue really matters. But that also means what’s running in production at 5pm on December 23rd is what you’re riding out the storm with. There’s no patching or hotfixing your way out of a bottleneck once you’re under fire.


### The Part Nobody Budgets For


The fraud-prevention industry has been saying this for a while, outside of gaming entirely: bots find it easier to hide when the traffic is heavy.[Forter](https://www.forter.com/blog/top-5-holiday-season-fraud-trends/) has tracked this pattern for years, and their data shows fraud attacks climbing 15-30% during the holiday season compared to the rest of the year. But a flood of real holiday shoppers pushes the overall fraud percentage back down, even while the raw number of attacks climbs.


In gaming,[account takeover](https://www.fastly.com/learning/security/what-is-an-account-takeover) reaches straight past the password to whatever’s attached to that account. Stored payment methods, in-game currency, skins and items with real resale value. Sometimes years of progress a player isn’t getting back. A compromised account during peak week rarely stops at one bad transaction. The real cost shows up later, with a player that is never going to spend anything on your game again.


This is even harder to catch in gaming than it is for a typical online store. Credential stuffing attacks against gaming platforms[rarely look like](https://www.fastly.com/blog/credential-stuffing-real-boss-fight-for-gaming-platforms) a single attacker hammering a login page. Attackers tend to skip the main web portal entirely, going straight for the PC, mobile companion, and console APIs that power matchmaking, inventory sync, and progression instead. During a normal week, that’s already a lot of surface area to watch. During peak week, it’s the same surface area buried under ten times the usual volume.


A studio catches an attack like that when the system absorbing the spike and the system watching for threats see the same traffic at the same moment. If they don’t, each is working from an incomplete picture.


## What Readiness Actually Looks Like


A surge shouldn’t decide whether your platform stays up, no matter if it’s legitimate traffic, an attack, or some mix of both. Load balancing and traffic distribution at the edge absorb that surge at the network layer, so your platform stays available and your users keep getting responses.


Visibility matters just as much. A 5xx spike and a login anomaly are often the same event – but only if someone’s actually watching both at once. Real-time log streaming, the kind of tools like[Fastly’s Log Explorer](https://www.fastly.com/products/load-balancing) are built for, is what turns a traffic surge and a login anomaly into one signal instead of two separate alerts that don’t get connected until a player posts about it on January 2nd.


Then there’s the traffic itself. A credential stuffing script doesn’t take a holiday. It just keeps hammering the same login endpoint with every combination it’s got.[Edge rate limiting](https://docs.fastly.com/products/edge-rate-limiting) caps how many requests any one client can make before it ever reaches your origin. A player who mistypes their password twice won’t notice. A script running through a few thousand combinations will.


And when that signal does get flagged, it has to be acted on without a human in the loop first: automated bot detection and WAF rules that trigger at the edge. They should be fast enough that ownership never becomes a question and dynamic enough to know the difference between a human player and a bot. Detection that’s too blunt creates its own readiness failure. A rigid, rule-based WAF can lock out legitimate players as easily as it stops attackers, one overly aggressive rule is all it takes to block a wave of new console registrations on Christmas morning. Readiness means catching the attack without punishing the players you’re protecting.


## Ready, Not Just Prepared


That’s the actual bar for readiness this December: a system that catches a credential stuffing attempt without first needing to guess whether the traffic spike is real.
